title: Japji 16–19, whole
hookLine: the countless, and the Name through letters
tomorrow: after the countless, what does the Japji say washes a mind clean?

cards: Ever tried counting the stars on a clear night and given up somewhere past the first handful? Pauri seventeen of the Japji opens with a word that gives up counting on purpose: asankh, countless.
Asankh jap, asankh bhaau: countless prayers, countless loves. Pauri eighteen turns it around: countless fools, countless thieves. Pauri nineteen: countless names, countless places.
What do you do with a list that can't end?

teach.b: Pauri sixteen sets the stage: panch parvaan panch pardhaan, the chosen ones are accepted and honored.
And the old picture of a bull holding up the earth gets a new reading: the bull is dharam, righteousness, the son of compassion, held in place by the thread of contentment.
Then the counting starts, and breaks. Countless devotions, countless scholars.

teach.h: NANAK, THE LOWLY, IN THE LIST.
teach.b: Countless cruel ones too, and Guru Nanak, after naming them, calls himself the lowly one, as if setting himself inside the list. Then pauri nineteen turns: akharee naam, akharee saalaah.
Through letters, the Name; through letters, praise. A creation too big to count is still sung in letters, the small marks this year began with.
Each of these pauris closes on the same refrain, in paraphrase: what power have I to describe your creation? Whatever pleases you is good; you are forever, Formless One.

how: In the morning Japji, Sikhs recite pauris sixteen to nineteen in order, each closing on the same refrain of praise for the Formless One.

o: a hymn of sixteen lines sung at weddings
pauris sixteen to nineteen: dharam and the countless
the sixteen virtues a Sikh tries to practice

games.q: the summit so far — tap the pairs.

s: pauri sixteen says a bull holds up the earth
it says the bull is dharam, the son of compassion, held by the thread of contentment.
akharee naam means through letters, the Name
pauri nineteen: through letters, the Name; through letters, praise.
Guru Nanak lists countless fools and leaves himself out
he calls himself the lowly one, as if inside the list.

games.q: a caption under a photo of the night sky says: 'the universe is too big to mean anything.' what would pauri nineteen say?
o: too big to count, and still sung through letters: the countless has a Name.
it's smaller than it looks; count carefully and it stops being countless.
nothing: the Japji speaks about prayer, never about the creation.
games.why: pauris seventeen to nineteen give up counting on purpose, then turn: akharee naam, through letters, the Name.

practice: Count slowly on your fingers, one breath for each thing you're grateful for today: a person, a meal, a quiet minute, anything at all. When your fingers run out, keep going without counting, and notice that the list doesn't end.

wordCard.voice: Japji 16. Pauris sixteen to nineteen, read whole: the bull that is dharam, the countless, and the Name sung through letters.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: countless, without number. it opens Japji pauris seventeen to nineteen.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the countless, sung through a handful of letters. Four of the summit, and a week counted.
